paras: The 1903 Bronx race riot was an outbreak of crowd violence against Black people near 155th Street and Washington Avenue in the Bronx, New York, on August 15, 1903, after a white man, John Finnessy, was stabbed outside a saloon, reportedly by a Black man who escaped. White men chased the assailant, and both reporting papers said four uninvolved Black men were attacked in the saloon until police rescued them.
Both accounts trace the trouble to a quarrel that evening in Gustave Kanze's saloon, over a bill (New-York Tribune) or Finnessy's spilled drink (New York Herald).

Later a group of Black men gathered opposite the saloon, and one came to the door, where Finnessy was stabbed (Tribune) or, after throwing the man down, cut with a razor (Herald). Men from the saloon, armed with billiard cues and bottles, chased him shouting, the Tribune said, "Kill him! Kill that nigger!"

According to the Tribune, about 150 white men, joined by neighborhood laborers, then beat and cut Black men and drove Black residents indoors; some Black residents came out armed. Policeman Belton of the Morrisania station called out the reserves. As the crowd returned, a dozen men set upon four Black men in Kanze's saloon until police broke in and led them away.

Finnessy was taken to Lebanon Hospital with slim chances; Captain Byrne sent a squad to capture the assailant and "prevent any harm coming to him." No report of an arrest, of Finnessy's fate, or of charges against the attackers was found.

Both stories ran on August 16 under headlines leading with the wounded white man: "RACE WAR IN THE BRONX" (Tribune) and "HUNDREDS JOIN IN BRONX RACE RIOTS" (Herald). Both relied on saloon patrons and police, yet both said the four men beaten had no part in the stabbing; the Herald wrote that several Black men "were saved from the vengeance of a crowd." No Black-press account was found.
The papers differ on the weapon (knife or razor), the crowd's size (about 150 or nearly 100), and who struck first; no account from the Black men involved appears.

bases: After the stabbing, a crowd of white men hunted Black people through the neighborhood, beating them and driving them into their homes [A1], and a dozen men attacked four Black men in the saloon who had no part in the trouble [A1, A2].
Two independently written New York reports of the same morning agree on the stabbing, the white pursuit, the police reserves, and the attack on four uninvolved Black men in Kanze's saloon [A1, A2].

accounts.label: Tribune (saloon patrons and police)
accounts.gist: Two Black men quarrelled with Kanze over a bill and threatened him; their companion stabbed Finnessy at the door, after which about 150 white men hunted and beat Black people all night in fighting in which both sides were armed.

accounts.label: Herald (saloon patrons and police)
accounts.gist: Black men jostled Finnessy in the saloon and were thrown out; when one later dared the white men outside, Finnessy threw him down and was cut with a razor; nearly 100 men pursued in vain, and four Black men were rescued from a dozen attackers.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'RACE WAR IN THE BRONX / NEGRO CUTS WHITE MAN', printed the crowd's shouts including a slur, described the white men falling on outnumbered Black men 'yelling triumphantly', and noted that the four men in the saloon 'knew nothing of the trouble'.
The Herald headlined 'HUNDREDS JOIN IN BRONX RACE RIOTS' and a 'General Fight with Negroes', while saying several Black men 'were saved from the vengeance of a crowd' by the reserves.

conflicts.note: Both reports are same-day and secondhand; neither is clearly better.

Around Gustave Kanze's saloon at 155th Street and Washington Avenue, the Bronx, New York City; pursuit toward Jerome Avenue

Unnamed Black men and residents beaten and cut by the white crowd, including the dozen men who had been with the assailant and four Black men who entered the saloon afterward; John Finnessy, a white man, was the stabbing victim whose wounding set off the attacks
